screens.title: Final Examination and Answer Key
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. This final chapter brings together the central ideas you have practiced across the specialization. We'll revisit kinematics and transforms, control inputs for aerial and ground platforms, path planning tradeoffs, models for legged locomotion, camera calibration, and probabilistic filters. You will also step through targeted code-analysis problems that expose common implementation pitfalls, and a practical design for a two-wheeled balancing robot that integrates control and estimation. Working through these questions helps you check depth of understanding and prepares you for system-level design where multiple topics interact. For example, a mobile inverted pendulum requires modeling, cascade control design, sensor fusion with an Extended Kalman Filter, and attention to actuator limits. The answer key shows correct choices and concise reasoning; use it to diagnose misconceptions and to rehearse the mental models behind each algorithm. As you move forward, ask yourself: which core assumption would break on my robot, and how would I adapt the algorithm in response?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we set clear objectives so you can check your readiness. First, be able to explain homogeneous transformations and compose poses reliably; this matters because frame chaining underlies kinematics and sensor registration. Second, diagnose estimator choices: describe when a Kalman Filter suffices, when an EKF is required, and when a particle filter is the right global-localization tool. Third, judge planning tradeoffs: articulate why A* uses heuristics to reduce explored nodes and where Dijkstra is still appropriate. Fourth, design and simulate a control system: specify an inner balance controller and an outer position loop, and implement an EKF that fuses noisy IMU and encoder data. Each objective links a precise skill to how you would use it on a real robot, and together they cover reasoning, analysis, and system integration you need for final projects.

screens.title: Homogeneous Transformation Matrices
screens.narratorSegment: A homogeneous transformation matrix is a 4-by-4 matrix that combines rotation and translation so you can chain coordinate-frame conversions via matrix multiplication. It extends a 3-by-3 rotation matrix with a 3-by-1 translation vector and a final row to preserve affine properties. This single structure simplifies forward kinematics: instead of applying rotation then translation separately, you multiply successive transforms to move from base to end-effector. A concrete example is composing a robot arm joint rotation and the following link translation to compute the end-effector pose relative to the base. A common misconception is thinking homogeneous matrices only rotate or only translate; they do both and must maintain the upper-left block as a valid rotation matrix with orthonormal columns. Another pitfall is using the wrong multiplication order—frame chaining is not commutative. Key practices: represent poses as 4x4 transforms, validate rotation blocks are orthonormal, and test by transforming a known point through a chain of transforms and checking expected coordinates. Takeaway: homogeneous transforms let you treat poses uniformly as matrix multiplications, making frame composition straightforward and less error-prone when done carefully. Homogeneous Transformation Matrices means use 4×4 homogeneous matrices to compose rotations and translations and validate rotation orthonormality.. In practical terms, combine rotation and translation into a single matrix operation.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Homogeneous Transformation Matrices
Homogeneous Transformation Matrices
Combine rotation and translation into one matrix
Definition
A 4×4 matrix consisting of a 3×3 rotation block R, a translation vector t, and a final row [0 0 0 1]. It maps homogeneous coordinates from one frame to another.
Properties to check:
  • Rotation block must be orthonormal: R R' = I.
  • Determinant of R should be +1 for a proper rotation.
  • Chain transforms by multiplication: T_ab = T_aB * T_Bb.
Concrete Example
Given a joint rotation about z by 30 degrees and a translation of 0.5 m along x, build the 4×4 transform and apply it to the end-effector point expressed in the link frame to get base coordinates.
Key Takeaway

Treat poses as homogeneous matrices for consistent and testable frame composition. Always verify the rotation block.

Visual
Pose T = [R t; 0 1]
% Example 4x4 homogeneous transform
R = [ cos(theta) -sin(theta) 0;
      sin(theta)  cos(theta) 0;
      0           0          1 ];
t = [0.5; 0; 0];
T = [R, t; 0 0 0 1];
% Transform point p_local to p_world
p_local = [0.1; 0; 0; 1];
p_world = T * p_local;
Common Misconception
Multiplying transforms in the wrong order yields incorrect frames. Verify with a known point to catch order errors.

screens.title: Quadrotor Yaw Control
screens.narratorSegment: Yaw rotation in a quadrotor is produced by creating a torque around the vehicle's vertical axis. A typical quad has two rotors spinning clockwise and two spinning counterclockwise; by changing the balance between clockwise and counterclockwise rotor speeds you produce a net reaction torque that rotates the vehicle in yaw. For example, increasing the speed of clockwise rotors while decreasing the counterclockwise ones produces a clockwise yaw moment. A common misconception is to think total thrust changes cause yaw; increasing total thrust primarily affects altitude, not yaw. Another detail: mixers must preserve overall thrust when commanding yaw so altitude control remains stable—practical controllers usually add equal-and-opposite adjustments to pairs of motors to generate yaw while maintaining lift. When designing control inputs, respect actuator limits and include saturation checks to avoid commanding impossible motor speeds. Takeaway: yaw is achieved by differential torque between opposing rotors, so controllers should allocate motor commands to produce the desired yaw moment while maintaining net thrust for altitude. Quadrotor Yaw Control means differential thrust between clockwise and counterclockwise rotors creates net torque about the vertical axis, producing yaw.. In practical terms, how differential rotor thrusts generate yaw rotation.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Quadrotor Yaw Control
Quadrotor Yaw Control
Differential torque between rotors produces yaw.
Principle
Rotors spinning in opposite directions create reaction torques. Yaw is the net torque about the vertical axis produced by differential rotor speeds.
  • Equal net motor speeds → no yaw torque, altitude changes only.
  • Increase CW motors, decrease CCW motors to yaw CW, preserving net thrust keeps altitude steady.
  • Mixer logic maps desired yaw moment to motor speed offsets subject to saturation limits.
Controller Note
Always command motor offsets that sum to zero when producing yaw, unless you intentionally change altitude.
Example Mixer
% Mixer pseudocode
% u_thrust: total thrust command
% u_roll, u_pitch, u_yaw: moment commands
m1 = u_thrust/4 - u_roll/2 + u_pitch/2 + u_yaw/4; % front-left
m2 = u_thrust/4 + u_roll/2 + u_pitch/2 - u_yaw/4; % front-right
m3 = u_thrust/4 + u_roll/2 - u_pitch/2 + u_yaw/4; % rear-right
m4 = u_thrust/4 - u_roll/2 - u_pitch/2 - u_yaw/4; % rear-left
% Constrain motor commands to min/max
Common Mistake
Changing all motors together changes altitude, not yaw. Use differential offsets to isolate yaw torque.

screens.title: A* versus Dijkstra for Pathfinding
screens.narratorSegment: A* and Dijkstra are graph search algorithms for finding shortest paths, but they differ in how they explore the search space. Dijkstra's algorithm expands nodes in increasing distance from the start and guarantees shortest paths on graphs with nonnegative weights, but it does not use information about the goal. A* augments the cost-to-come with a heuristic estimate of cost-to-go, steering exploration toward promising regions; when the heuristic is admissible and consistent, A* still finds optimal paths but typically inspects far fewer nodes. A concrete example: on a 2D grid with Euclidean distances, Dijkstra explores concentric rings outward, while A* with straight-line distance focuses on nodes nearer the goal corridor. A misconception is believing A* always uses less memory than Dijkstra—A* can still use large memory depending on branching and heuristic quality. Choose Dijkstra when you need many-source shortest paths or have no admissible heuristic. Choose A* to speed single-source single-goal queries using a reliable heuristic. Takeaway: heuristic guidance is the practical advantage of A*; verify admissibility to retain optimality. A* versus Dijkstra for Pathfinding means a* uses admissible heuristics to focus search, typically visiting fewer nodes than dijkstra while still guaranteeing optimality when conditions hold.. In practical terms, how heuristics guide search and when to prefer each algorithm.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › A* vs Dijkstra
A* vs Dijkstra
Heuristic guidance and search efficiency
Dijkstra
Expands nodes by increasing known cost from start. No heuristic; explores uniformly until goal cost is settled.
  • Guaranteed optimality on nonnegative weights.
  • Good for many-source shortest paths or when heuristic is unavailable.
A*
Adds heuristic h(n) to cost g(n) to estimate full cost f(n)=g(n)+h(n). When h is admissible, A* is optimal and usually more efficient.
  • Quality of h determines efficiency.
  • Non-admissible heuristics can be faster but lose optimality.
Concrete Example
On a grid, use Euclidean distance as an admissible heuristic for A*. You will see A* explore nodes near the straight-line corridor between start and goal while Dijkstra explores outward rings.
Misconception
A* does not always use less memory; poor heuristics or high branching factor can still produce large open sets.
Key Takeaway

Prefer A* for single-goal searches when you have an admissible heuristic. Use Dijkstra for complete, uninformed shortest-path needs.

screens.title: Spring-Loaded Inverted Pendulum (SLIP) Model
screens.narratorSegment: The Spring-Loaded Inverted Pendulum, or SLIP, is a reduced-order model used to capture the essential dynamics of running and hopping. It represents the body mass as a point mass atop a massless spring leg. During stance, the spring stores and releases mechanical energy, producing the bounce characteristic of running. The SLIP captures gait dynamics such as stance-to-flight transitions, stride frequency, and energy exchange without modeling every joint. A practical example: tune spring stiffness and touchdown angle to achieve a desired stride length and stable periodic gait in a legged robot. A common misconception is that SLIP models legged robots fully; it ignores actuator dynamics, foot geometry, and multi-segment legs. Use SLIP for intuition and first-order stability analysis, then add higher-fidelity models for controller design. Takeaway: SLIP provides a tractable, analytically useful lens on running dynamics, helping you design controllers and reason about energy storage in legged locomotion. Spring-Loaded Inverted Pendulum (SLIP) Model means slip uses a point mass and spring leg to model energy exchange and gait dynamics for running and hopping analysis.. In practical terms, a simple dynamical model for running and hopping behaviors.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › SLIP Model
Spring-Loaded Inverted Pendulum (SLIP)
A minimal model for running and hopping
Model
Point mass body atop a massless spring leg. Dynamics alternate between flight and stance phases where the spring compresses and extends.
  • Parameters: mass, leg stiffness, touchdown angle.
  • Outputs: stride length, apex height, stability of periodic motion.
Usage
Analyze gait stability, design touchdown control laws, and estimate energy budgets for legged robots.
Concrete Example
Adjust leg stiffness to change return energy: stiffer springs increase bounce but may reduce stability; softer springs reduce peak forces but need active control to maintain stride length.
Key Takeaway

Use SLIP for first-order gait design and intuition, then refine with multi-segment dynamics for control implementation.

screens.title: Camera Intrinsic Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Intrinsic camera parameters characterize how a camera maps 3D rays into image pixels independent of where the camera is in the world. They include focal length, principal point, and distortion coefficients. Focal length scales coordinates from camera units to pixels; the principal point locates the optical center in the image plane; distortion coefficients model lens nonidealities such as radial and tangential distortion. A concrete case: undistorting feature measurements requires knowing intrinsics so triangulation yields correct 3D geometry. A common misunderstanding is to confuse intrinsics with extrinsics—the camera's pose in the world. Intrinsics are internal to the camera and remain the same when the camera moves; extrinsics change with pose. Calibration procedures estimate intrinsics by observing known patterns and minimizing reprojection error. Takeaway: accurate intrinsics are essential for reliable metric reconstruction and any vision-based control that depends on real-world scaling and geometry. In practical terms, what intrinsics describe and why they matter for vision tasks.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Camera Intrinsics
Camera Intrinsic Parameters
Focal length, principal point, and distortion
What intrinsics capture
  • Focal length: scales projection to pixel units.
  • Principal point: image center offset from sensor origin.
  • Distortion: models radial and tangential nonlinearities.
Why it matters
Without correct intrinsics, triangulation and pose estimation will be biased and reprojection errors increase. For metric tasks, accurate intrinsics are required to recover real-world scale when used with other sensors.
Calibration Note
Calibration minimizes reprojection error over many views of a known pattern to estimate focal length, principal point, and distortion terms.
Key Takeaway

Treat intrinsics as fixed camera properties; calibrate before metric reconstruction or sensor fusion tasks that assume correct projection models.

screens.title: Kalman Filter: Prediction and Update
screens.narratorSegment: The Kalman Filter operates in two repeated steps: prediction and update. In the prediction step, the filter applies the system dynamics to estimate the next state and propagates uncertainty through the covariance using P = A P A' + Q. This projects current uncertainty forward according to the linear model and adds process noise. Then the update step incorporates a measurement: compute the innovation, form the Kalman gain, and correct the state estimate and covariance. The Kalman gain balances trust between prediction and observation based on their uncertainties. A concrete example: tracking a 1D position and velocity where A implements constant-velocity motion; omission of the A' term in covariance prediction yields incorrect uncertainty evolution and can lead to overconfident updates. A key misconception is that the Kalman Filter directly applies to nonlinear dynamics—it does not. The EKF linearizes about the current estimate to apply the same two-step logic. Takeaway: always implement P prediction as A P A' + Q, and understand how the Kalman gain blends model and sensor information. Kalman Filter: Prediction and Update means prediction uses dynamics and p = a p a' + q; update fuses measurements via the kalman gain to reduce uncertainty.. In practical terms, two-step recursion that propagates and corrects state estimates.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Kalman Filter Steps
Kalman Filter: Prediction and Update
Understand covariance propagation and measurement fusion
Prediction
Compute x_prior = A x + B u and P_prior = A P A' + Q. This step moves the estimate forward using the dynamics and inflates uncertainty by process noise.
Check: missing A' in P update is a common bug that misprojects uncertainty.
Update
Compute Kalman gain K = P_prior H' (H P_prior H' + R)^{-1}, then x_post = x_prior + K (z - H x_prior), P_post = (I - K H) P_prior.
Kalman gain determines weight on the measurement vs. prediction.
Concrete Bug Example
% Incorrect covariance update
x = A * x + B * u;
P = A * P + Q;   % BUG: missing A'
% Correct:
P = A * P * A' + Q;
Misconception
Believing covariance prediction is A P + Q underestimates how dynamics rotate uncertainty. Implement the full A P A' term.

screens.title: Particle Filters and Resampling
screens.narratorSegment: A particle filter represents a belief over state using many weighted samples, or particles. Each particle is a hypothesis about the true state, and weights reflect likelihood under the observation model. The resampling step draws particles with replacement proportional to weight, discarding low-weight particles and duplicating high-weight ones; this concentrates computational effort where probability mass lies. Consider global localization: if the robot's initial position is unknown, a particle filter can initialize particles uniformly across the map and gradually focus them through motion and sensing. EKF cannot represent multimodal beliefs because it restricts the belief to a single Gaussian. A common pitfall in resampling is sample impoverishment: repeatedly resampling without adding process noise can collapse diversity. Remedies include adding jitter or using systematic resampling combined with motion propagation. Takeaway: particle filters are essential when the state distribution is multimodal or non-Gaussian, and careful resampling strategy preserves diversity while focusing computation on high-probability regions. Particle Filters and Resampling means resampling draws particles proportional to weight to focus hypotheses; add noise or effective-sample-size heuristics to avoid impoverishment.. In practical terms, why resampling concentrates high-likelihood hypotheses and when to use particles.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Particle Filters
Particle Filters and Resampling
Represent arbitrary distributions with weighted samples
Mechanics
Particles propagate under motion, weight by likelihood of measurements, then resample. Resampling replicates high-likelihood particles proportional to weight.
  • Initialize widely for global localization.
  • Resample when effective sample size falls below a threshold.
Pitfalls & Remedies
Avoid sample impoverishment by injecting small process noise after resampling, or use stratified/systematic resampling for lower variance.
Concrete Example
For a robot that doesn't know its starting pose, scatter many particles over the map. As the robot senses features, particle weights identify hypotheses consistent with measurements and resampling concentrates particles on plausible poses.
Key Takeaway

Use particles for multimodal beliefs and global localization, and manage diversity through resampling heuristics and process noise.

screens.title: Odometry Drift: Causes and Mitigation
screens.narratorSegment: Odometry estimates pose by integrating wheel motions, but it drifts because errors accumulate over time. Primary causes include wheel slip, uneven terrain, and encoder quantization; each introduces small errors that grow as the robot moves. For instance, a small slip during a turn yields a heading error that biases subsequent position estimates. Effective mitigation strategies include fusing absolute sensors such as GPS or landmarks, using visual odometry to bound drift, and improving wheel contact models to detect slip. Kalman or particle filters can fuse noisy measurements to reduce long-term drift by periodically correcting the odometry estimate. A common misconception is that simply increasing encoder resolution will eliminate drift; while higher resolution reduces quantization error, it does not address systematic slips or terrain-induced errors. Takeaway: odometry is useful for short-term motion estimates, but robust navigation requires sensor fusion and periodic absolute corrections to prevent unbounded drift. Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Odometry Drift
Odometry Drift: Causes and Mitigation
Small errors accumulate—plan for correction
Common Causes
  • Wheel slip from low friction or obstacles.
  • Uneven terrain creating varying effective wheel radii.
  • Encoder quantization limiting resolution.
Mitigation
  • Fuse odometry with absolute sensors or visual landmarks.
  • Use state estimators to blend short-term odometry with long-term corrections.
  • Detect slip and reduce reliance on encoder-only updates during those intervals.
Key Takeaway

Odometry is short-term reliable. Prevent long-term drift by fusing absolute measurements and detecting slip to avoid compounding errors.

screens.title: Structure from Motion: Scale Ambiguity and Bundle Adjustment
screens.narratorSegment: Monocular Structure from Motion reconstructs 3D structure and camera motion from image sequences, but it cannot determine absolute scale without additional information. The essential matrix or relative pose recovery yields translations up to scale because a scaled 3D scene projects to the same image observations under scaled translations. For example, a camera that moves twice the distance through space produces equivalent bearing measurements if scene geometry is scaled down accordingly. Bundle adjustment addresses accumulated estimation errors by jointly optimizing camera poses and 3D point coordinates to minimize reprojection error across all images. It is a nonlinear least-squares refinement that significantly improves accuracy after initial pairwise estimates and triangulation. A common mistake is to trust pairwise triangulations without global refinement; bundle adjustment corrects those local inconsistencies. Takeaway: monocular SfM gives geometry up to scale; use additional sensors, known-size objects, or stereo baselines to recover absolute scale, and run bundle adjustment to refine all parameters jointly. In practical terms, why monocular sfm lacks absolute scale and how bundle adjustment refines reconstructions.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Structure from Motion
Structure from Motion: Scale & Bundle Adjustment
Monocular SfM yields scale ambiguity; bundle adjustment refines all variables.
Scale Ambiguity
The essential matrix determines translation direction but not its magnitude. Monocular pipelines therefore recover structure up to an unknown scale factor.
Resolve scale with stereo baselines, known object sizes, or inertial measurements fused with visual data.
Bundle Adjustment
A nonlinear optimization that jointly refines camera parameters and 3D points by minimizing reprojection error across all observations. It corrects accumulated pairwise errors.
Key Takeaway

Expect monocular SfM to lack metric scale. Use auxiliary measurements or bundle adjustment plus external priors to recover absolute geometry reliably.

screens.title: Potential Field Controller: Local Minima and Influence Radius
screens.narratorSegment: The potential field controller computes attractive forces toward the goal and repulsive forces from obstacles, then sums them to obtain a navigation force. The supplied MATLAB code uses an attractive term proportional to distance and repulsive terms proportional to inverse cubic distance, applied for every obstacle without a finite influence radius. This design can trap a robot in a local minimum where attractive and repulsive forces cancel, preventing progress. Also, unbounded repulsion means distant obstacles still affect the force, which is inefficient and unexpected. A concrete fix is to apply a finite influence distance d0: only compute repulsive forces when the robot is within d0 of an obstacle, and scale the magnitude smoothly to zero at d0. Additionally, local minima can be mitigated with escape strategies such as random perturbations, harmonic potentials, or hybrid planners that switch to search when trapped. Takeaway: potential fields are simple and useful, but practical implementations require limited influence radii and escape heuristics to handle local minima and computational cost. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Potential Field Analysis
Potential Field Controller: Code Walkthrough
Find the local minimum and influence-radius issues in the MATLAB example
Original Code
function F = controller(q, q_goal, obstacles)
    F = -2 * (q - q_goal);
    for i = 1:length(obstacles)
        d = norm(q - obstacles{i});
        F = F + 10 * (q - obstacles{i}) / d^3;
    end
end
Diagnosis & Fix
Problems: no finite influence radius, unbounded repulsion, and local minima. Fix by using influence radius d0 and zeroing repulsion beyond it; add a small jitter or planner fallback to escape minima.
% Suggested change (pseudocode)
d0 = 1.0; % influence radius
F = -ka * (q - q_goal);
for each obstacle
  d = norm(q - obs);
  if d < d0
    F = F + kr * (q - obs) * (1/d - 1/d0) / (d^2);
  end
end
Key Takeaway

Practical potential fields need bounded influence and escape strategies; otherwise local minima and long-range distortions will block navigation.

screens.title: Mobile Inverted Pendulum: Design and EKF Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a mobile inverted pendulum combines linearized dynamics, cascade control, and sensor fusion. The inner loop keeps the pendulum angle near zero using high-gain balance control, while the outer loop commands a desired position by producing a small desired tilt. For the inner controller, proportional-derivative gains on angle and angular rate stabilize the pendulum; for the outer loop, a PD on position produces a target tilt that the inner loop tracks. Implement an Extended Kalman Filter to fuse noisy IMU measurements of angle and angular rate with wheel encoder velocity: predict the state with the linearized A and B matrices, and update with measurement model H. The provided MATLAB example in the chapter shows a working simulation: tune Kp_theta and Kd_theta for tight balance, Kp_x and Kd_x for smooth position control, and bound motor commands. Common pitfalls include not limiting desired tilt and forgetting sensor noise covariances in EKF; choose Q and R to reflect process and sensor noise. Takeaway: the cascade architecture separates fast balancing from slower position regulation, and the EKF provides robust state estimates under sensor noise, enabling reliable motion to the target position.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Mobile Inverted Pendulum
Design: Two-Wheeled Balancing Robot
Cascade controller and EKF integration
Controller Architecture
Outer loop: position PD computes a desired tilt. Inner loop: high-gain PD on pendulum angle tracks desired tilt and stabilizes balance. Limit desired tilt to small angles to keep linearization valid.
  • Inner gains: Kp_theta, Kd_theta control fast balancing.
  • Outer gains: Kp_x, Kd_x produce smooth motion commands mapped to tilt.
  • Saturate motor commands to safe bounds.
EKF Estimator
State vector [x; x_dot; theta; theta_dot]. Use A and B from linearization to predict and H to update with IMU and encoder measurements. Carefully set Q and R to reflect process and measurement noise.
Simulation Snippet
% EKF prediction
x_pred = x_est + (A * x_est + B * u) * dt;
F = eye(4) + A * dt;
P_pred = F * P * F' + Q * dt;
% EKF update
K = P_pred * H' / (H * P_pred * H' + R);
x_est = x_pred + K * (z - H * x_pred);
P = (eye(4) - K * H) * P_pred;
Key Takeaway

Split control into inner balance and outer motion loops, fuse sensors with an EKF, and simulate with realistic noise to tune gains and covariances before deployment.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. This final chapter brings together the central ideas you have practiced across the specialization. We'll revisit kinematics and transforms, control inputs for aerial and ground platforms, path planning tradeoffs, models for legged locomotion, camera calibration, and probabilistic filters. You will also step through targeted code-analysis problems that expose common implementation pitfalls, and a practical design for a two-wheeled balancing robot that integrates control and estimation. Working through these questions helps you check depth of understanding and prepares you for system-level design where multiple topics interact. For example, a mobile inverted pendulum requires modeling, cascade control design, sensor fusion with an Extended Kalman Filter, and attention to actuator limits. The answer key shows correct choices and concise reasoning; use it to diagnose misconceptions and to rehearse the mental models behind each algorithm. As you move forward, ask yourself: which core assumption would break on my robot, and how would I adapt the algorithm in response?

In this lesson we set clear objectives so you can check your readiness. First, be able to explain homogeneous transformations and compose poses reliably; this matters because frame chaining underlies kinematics and sensor registration. Second, diagnose estimator choices: describe when a Kalman Filter suffices, when an EKF is required, and when a particle filter is the right global-localization tool. Third, judge planning tradeoffs: articulate why A* uses heuristics to reduce explored nodes and where Dijkstra is still appropriate. Fourth, design and simulate a control system: specify an inner balance controller and an outer position loop, and implement an EKF that fuses noisy IMU and encoder data. Each objective links a precise skill to how you would use it on a real robot, and together they cover reasoning, analysis, and system integration you need for final projects.

This continuation focuses on applied reasoning and debugging. First, interpret sensory uncertainty: practice computing covariance propagation and spotting mistakes in covariance updates, such as omitting the A-transpose term. Second, reason about localization: understand resampling in particle filters and why that concentrates high-likelihood hypotheses. Third, evaluate perception algorithms: explain why monocular Structure from Motion cannot recover absolute scale and why bundle adjustment refines camera poses and 3D points. Fourth, analyze controller code: detect local minima in potential field methods and design finite influence radii or escape strategies. These objectives are practical: they help you read algorithm outputs for signs of failure, and choose corrective measures rather than guessing. As you study, try to explain each failure mode out loud and propose a small test that would reveal it on a real robot.

A homogeneous transformation matrix is a 4-by-4 matrix that combines rotation and translation so you can chain coordinate-frame conversions via matrix multiplication. It extends a 3-by-3 rotation matrix with a 3-by-1 translation vector and a final row to preserve affine properties. This single structure simplifies forward kinematics: instead of applying rotation then translation separately, you multiply successive transforms to move from base to end-effector. A concrete example is composing a robot arm joint rotation and the following link translation to compute the end-effector pose relative to the base. A common misconception is thinking homogeneous matrices only rotate or only translate; they do both and must maintain the upper-left block as a valid rotation matrix with orthonormal columns. Another pitfall is using the wrong multiplication order—frame chaining is not commutative. Key practices: represent poses as 4x4 transforms, validate rotation blocks are orthonormal, and test by transforming a known point through a chain of transforms and checking expected coordinates. Takeaway: homogeneous transforms let you treat poses uniformly as matrix multiplications, making frame composition straightforward and less error-prone when done carefully. Homogeneous Transformation Matrices means use 4×4 homogeneous matrices to compose rotations and translations and validate rotation orthonormality.. In practical terms, combine rotation and translation into a single matrix operation.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Yaw rotation in a quadrotor is produced by creating a torque around the vehicle's vertical axis. A typical quad has two rotors spinning clockwise and two spinning counterclockwise; by changing the balance between clockwise and counterclockwise rotor speeds you produce a net reaction torque that rotates the vehicle in yaw. For example, increasing the speed of clockwise rotors while decreasing the counterclockwise ones produces a clockwise yaw moment. A common misconception is to think total thrust changes cause yaw; increasing total thrust primarily affects altitude, not yaw. Another detail: mixers must preserve overall thrust when commanding yaw so altitude control remains stable—practical controllers usually add equal-and-opposite adjustments to pairs of motors to generate yaw while maintaining lift. When designing control inputs, respect actuator limits and include saturation checks to avoid commanding impossible motor speeds. Takeaway: yaw is achieved by differential torque between opposing rotors, so controllers should allocate motor commands to produce the desired yaw moment while maintaining net thrust for altitude. Quadrotor Yaw Control means differential thrust between clockwise and counterclockwise rotors creates net torque about the vertical axis, producing yaw.. In practical terms, how differential rotor thrusts generate yaw rotation.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A* and Dijkstra are graph search algorithms for finding shortest paths, but they differ in how they explore the search space. Dijkstra's algorithm expands nodes in increasing distance from the start and guarantees shortest paths on graphs with nonnegative weights, but it does not use information about the goal. A* augments the cost-to-come with a heuristic estimate of cost-to-go, steering exploration toward promising regions; when the heuristic is admissible and consistent, A* still finds optimal paths but typically inspects far fewer nodes. A concrete example: on a 2D grid with Euclidean distances, Dijkstra explores concentric rings outward, while A* with straight-line distance focuses on nodes nearer the goal corridor. A misconception is believing A* always uses less memory than Dijkstra—A* can still use large memory depending on branching and heuristic quality. Choose Dijkstra when you need many-source shortest paths or have no admissible heuristic. Choose A* to speed single-source single-goal queries using a reliable heuristic. Takeaway: heuristic guidance is the practical advantage of A*; verify admissibility to retain optimality. A* versus Dijkstra for Pathfinding means a* uses admissible heuristics to focus search, typically visiting fewer nodes than dijkstra while still guaranteeing optimality when conditions hold.. The Spring-Loaded Inverted Pendulum, or SLIP, is a reduced-order model used to capture the essential dynamics of running and hopping. Intrinsic camera parameters characterize how a camera maps 3D rays into image pixels independent of where the camera is in the world. They include focal length, principal point, and distortion coefficients. The Kalman Filter operates in two repeated steps: prediction and update. In the prediction step, the filter applies the system dynamics to estimate the next state and propagates uncertainty through the covariance using P = A P A' + Q. This projects current uncertainty forward according to the linear model and adds process noise. Then the update step incorporates a measurement: compute the innovation, form the Kalman gain, and correct the state estimate and covariance. The Kalman gain balances trust between prediction and observation based on their uncertainties. A particle filter represents a belief over state using many weighted samples, or particles. Each particle is a hypothesis about the true state, and weights reflect likelihood under the observation model. The resampling step draws particles with replacement proportional to weight, discarding low-weight particles and duplicating high-weight ones; this concentrates computational effort where probability mass lies. Consider global localization: if the robot's initial position is unknown, a particle filter can initialize particles uniformly across the map and gradually focus them through motion and sensing. EKF cannot represent multimodal beliefs because it restricts the belief to a single Gaussian. Remedies include adding jitter or using systematic resampling combined with motion propagation. Takeaway: particle filters are essential when the state distribution is multimodal or non-Gaussian, and careful resampling strategy preserves diversity while focusing computation on high-probability regions. Odometry estimates pose by integrating wheel motions, but it drifts because errors accumulate over time. Primary causes include wheel slip, uneven terrain, and encoder quantization; each introduces small errors that grow as the robot moves. For instance, a small slip during a turn yields a heading error that biases subsequent position estimates. Effective mitigation strategies include fusing absolute sensors such as GPS or landmarks, using visual odometry to bound drift, and improving wheel contact models to detect slip. Kalman or particle filters can fuse noisy measurements to reduce long-term drift by periodically correcting the odometry estimate. A common misconception is that simply increasing encoder resolution will eliminate drift; while higher resolution reduces quantization error, it does not address systematic slips or terrain-induced errors. The potential field controller computes attractive forces toward the goal and repulsive forces from obstacles, then sums them to obtain a navigation force. The supplied MATLAB code uses an attractive term proportional to distance and repulsive terms proportional to inverse cubic distance, applied for every obstacle without a finite influence radius. This design can trap a robot in a local minimum where attractive and repulsive forces cancel, preventing progress. Also, unbounded repulsion means distant obstacles still affect the force, which is inefficient and unexpected. A concrete fix is to apply a finite influence distance d0: only compute repulsive forces when the robot is within d0 of an obstacle, and scale the magnitude smoothly to zero at d0. Additionally, local minima can be mitigated with escape strategies such as random perturbations, harmonic potentials, or hybrid planners that switch to search when trapped. Takeaway: potential fields are simple and useful, but practical implementations require limited influence radii and escape heuristics to handle local minima and computational cost.
